finding_dispositions.evidence: Fresh r5 verifier replay and targeted tests passed for no-follow initialization, fanout, and post-initialization objects/staging/locks/resources replacement. Descriptor-bound operations reject replaced attested ancestors before external mutation, and independent staging/final probes remained confined to isolated repository roots.

The freshly rerun clock regression passed: expiry observation persists repository-owned high-water state, and subsequent wall-clock rollback cannot revive an expired lease. Authoritative time decisions remain transactionally bound to the persisted high-water mark.

Fresh canonical resource-order and opposing-process regressions passed. Cross-token acquisition validates the global canonical sequence before mutation, and opposing two-process requests terminate without deadlock.

The fresh exact claim/reconciliation regression passed. Direct CommitBatch validation binds the complete ordered lease-resource set, fence tokens, task lease, and same-transaction event payload, including missing, extra, empty, stale, and wrong-lease rejection.

Fresh connection tests passed for doctor and backup read-only enforcement. Read-only URI, query_only, and deny-by-default authorizer reject direct writes and WITH-prefixed UPDATE, DELETE, and INSERT statements.

Fresh replay and recovery corruption tests passed. Event indexes, transaction revisions, transaction heads, and task/head state are validated against authoritative replay and fail closed on corruption.

Independent r5 separate-thread probes at object.after_staging_directory_fsync and object.after_publication raised ObjectIntegrityError, cleared wrong staging/final names, left no fresh available metadata, and retained no tampered bytes. Retained staging and final descriptors plus repeated inode/digest binding close the r3 available-wrong-bytes exploit.

Fresh-object probes at object.after_object_directory_fsync and object.before_metadata_commit now fail, clear wrong final and staging, and leave no metadata; post-commit replacement is quarantined. However, independent dedup probes first created an available object and then replaced its final during a second put at each of those two windows. Both calls raised ObjectIntegrityError and removed final/staging, but the preexisting database row remained state='available', now pointing to a missing file. The pre-transaction and transaction-internal mismatch handlers set cleanup_final without quarantining existing metadata.

findings.summary: Pre-transaction and transaction-window mismatch handling leaves preexisting deduplicated metadata available after deleting its final object.
findings.evidence: For both object.after_object_directory_fsync and object.before_metadata_commit, an independent probe first completed put_verified for a valid object and confirmed state='available'. During a second deduplicating put of the same bytes, a separate thread replaced the final name with tampered bytes at the selected barrier. put_verified correctly raised ObjectIntegrityError and cleared final and staging, but a database query still returned state='available' with the original size while the canonical final path no longer existed. The governing Spec and Test Plan require any already committed metadata implicated by a binding mismatch to become quarantined; the current gate combines basic dedup and fresh-object replacement tests but does not exercise this stateful composition.
findings.required_fix: On every post-publication pre-transaction or transaction-internal final binding mismatch, atomically quarantine any existing available metadata before or as part of safe wrong-final cleanup; preserve absent metadata for a fresh publication and quarantine post-commit mismatches. Add gate-bound separate-thread dedup regressions for object.after_object_directory_fsync and object.before_metadata_commit that first establish available metadata, then replace final during a second put and assert failure, empty staging, no wrong final, and state='quarantined'. Retain the fresh-object, publication, dedup-success, and 13-step-by-3-kind fault regressions.
